subject: physics
title: Magnetic fields and force on a current
key_idea: Moving charges and magnets make magnetic fields, drawn as field lines. A current-carrying wire in a field feels a force F = BIL sin θ, with direction from Fleming's left-hand rule. B is the force per unit current per unit length.

blocks.text: A magnetic field is a region where a magnet or a moving charge feels a force. We draw it with field lines.

items.meaning: A field of force produced by moving charges (currents) or by permanent magnets.
A line whose tangent shows the direction of the field. It points the way a free north pole would move.

items: Outside a magnet, field lines run from the north pole to the south pole.
Where lines are closer together the field is stronger.
Field lines never cross.
A uniform field has parallel, equally spaced lines.
Moving charges and permanent magnets both produce magnetic fields.
Field lines show direction and, by their spacing, strength.

blocks.text: A current in a wire makes its own magnetic field. The shape depends on how the wire is arranged.

rows: Concentric circles around the wire, getting further apart away from it
Circles around each part of the wire. Straight and strongest along the axis through the centre
Strong, uniform and parallel to the axis inside. Outside, like a bar magnet

items: Right-hand grip for a straight wire: thumb along the current, curled fingers show the field direction.
For a coil or solenoid: curl the fingers of the right hand the way the current goes round. The thumb points to the north end.
A solenoid has a north pole at one end and a south pole at the other.
A straight wire gives circular field lines.
A solenoid has a uniform field inside and a bar-magnet field outside.

blocks.text: A wire carrying a current in a magnetic field feels a force. The wire's own field interacts with the external field.

blocks.label: Force on a current-carrying wire
where: L = length of wire in the field (m)
θ = angle between the wire and the field

items: The force is greatest, F = BIL, when the wire is at right angles to the field.
The force is zero when the wire is parallel to the field.
Reversing the current or the field reverses the force.
The force is at right angles to both the field and the wire.

diagram.alt: An explorer activity on Fleming's left-hand rule. Tap each part of the left hand to see what it represents.
diagram.prompt: Hold your left hand with the thumb, first finger and second finger at right angles. Tap each part to see what it shows.

parts.name: Thumb
parts.detail: Points in the direction of the force (and so the motion) on the wire.

parts.name: First finger
parts.detail: Points in the direction of the magnetic field, from north to south.

parts.name: Second finger
parts.detail: Points in the direction of the conventional current, from positive to negative.

parts.name: The three together
parts.detail: They must be at right angles. If the wire is not at right angles to the field, use only the component of the field at right angles to the wire.

diagram.alt: A slider activity. Change the flux density, the current, the length of wire and the angle to the field and see the force on the wire.

inputs.label: Length of wire in the field

items: F = BIL sin θ.
Use Fleming's left-hand rule: thumb force, first finger field, second finger current.

sections.heading: Magnetic flux density and the tesla

blocks.text: The strength of a magnetic field is its magnetic flux density B. It is defined from the force on a wire.

blocks.label: Magnetic flux density (wire at right angles to the field)

items.meaning: The force acting per unit current per unit length on a wire placed at right angles to the field.
The flux density when a 1 m wire carrying 1 A at right angles to the field feels a force of 1 N. 1 T = 1 N A⁻¹ m⁻¹.

items: B is force per unit current per unit length, at right angles to the field.
The unit is the tesla, 1 T = 1 N A⁻¹ m⁻¹.

sections.heading: Measuring the force on a wire

blocks.text: A top-pan balance can measure a force on a wire, because the wire exerts an equal and opposite force on the magnets.

items.text: Put a pair of magnets on a yoke on the balance. Hold a straight wire horizontally between the poles, not touching the magnets.
Zero the balance with no current.
Pass a current through the wire. The reading changes by a mass m, so the force is F = mg.
Change the current, or the length of wire in the field, or the number of magnets, one at a time.

items: A graph of F against I is a straight line through the origin. Its gradient is BL.
A graph of F against L is a straight line through the origin. Its gradient is BI.
From the gradient, B = gradient ÷ L (or ÷ I).
The force on the wire is found from the change in balance reading, F = mg.
Straight-line graphs through the origin confirm F = BIL.

checks.q: A straight wire of length 0.15 m carries a current of 4.0 A at right angles to a uniform field of flux density 0.20 T. Calculate the force on the wire.
A wire of length 0.20 m carries 6.0 A in a uniform field of 0.50 T. The wire makes an angle of 30° with the field. Calculate the force on the wire.

checks.a: The tesla is the magnetic flux density at which a wire of length 1 m carrying a current of 1 A at right angles to the field experiences a force of 1 N.

items: A solenoid with a ferrous (iron) core has a much stronger field than the same solenoid with air inside.
The iron is magnetised by the current's field, and its own field adds to it.

blocks.text: Two long parallel wires each sit in the field of the other. That is the origin of the force between them.

items.text: Wire 1 makes a circular field. At wire 2 it is at right angles to the wire.
Wire 2 carries a current in that field, so it feels a force. Fleming's left-hand rule gives its direction.
Wire 2's field acts on wire 1 in the same way. The two forces are equal and opposite, by Newton's third law.

items: Currents in the same direction: the wires attract.
Currents in opposite directions: the wires repel.
The force gets smaller as the wires move further apart, because the field of a wire weakens with distance.
Each wire is in the other's field, so each feels a force.
Parallel currents attract. Opposite currents repel.
